I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel isolated and set apart from others
There is something about me that made the event happen
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

vignette: John is a 49-year-old North American male architect who recently witnessed a violent attack at his office building. The traumatic event has left him feeling overwhelmed and struggling to cope with daily life. John's wife describes how he has become increasingly withdrawn since the incident. The traumatic event occurred when John was leaving work one evening. He saw two employees in an altercation, which quickly escalated into a violent assault. One of them was struck repeatedly and fell unconscious while John stood frozen, unable to intervene effectively. This witnessing experience has deeply affected him, especially due to his inability to prevent the violence. Since then, John reports feeling constantly on edge, particularly when he encounters triggers such as scenes of violence, strong odors reminiscent of that night (like the smell of blood and sweat), and feelings of nausea. These triggers often plunge him into a state where he feels unsafe unless his back is against a wall and he can see everything in the room. He constantly scans for exits whenever he enters any building or room, believing that being aware of escape routes will help him feel more secure. John frequently relives the event, feeling like it is happening all over again when these triggers are present. He struggles to put the memories in sequence and often finds himself unable to articulate what happened. This inability to fully process the event has left him feeling confused and isolated from others. At times, he feels that there must be something inherently wrong with him for not being able to prevent or stop the violence. His negative appraisals—such as believing he is at fault and that he cannot protect himself or others—intensify his sense of threat. These beliefs make it hard for John to trust his own judgment, leading him to over-monitor his environment for potential dangers. This constant monitoring has led to a cycle where any perceived trigger exacerbates his fear and anxiety. John’s occupation as an architect places him in environments where he often encounters the smell of construction materials or the sight of workers in action, both of which remind him of the violent scene he witnessed. His heightened vigilance and need for safety have also affected his work interactions; he has become less willing to engage in collaborative brainstorming sessions, feeling that being surrounded by people makes him more vulnerable. The weight of these experiences is evident in how they have shaped John’s daily life. He finds it increasingly difficult to socialize or even go out alone because he fears encountering similar triggers and the accompanying sense of helplessness. What frightens him most is the fear that another such event could occur, leaving him feeling unable to protect himself or anyone else. Despite these challenges, John has recognized that his symptoms have become too burdensome, prompting him to seek psychological help. He hopes to regain a sense of control and be able to function without the constant dread of reliving the traumatic experience. His primary goal is to feel safe again and reconnect with others in meaningful ways.
